extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or advanced high-school students studying sequences, recurrences, and polynomials; math contest/problem-solving audience
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques, criteria, and canonical facts used to analyze sequences, recurrences, limits, periodicity, divisibility properties, and basic polynomial theory (division algorithm, roots, multiplicity, Vieta, roots of unity, cubic decomposition). Intended as a problem-solving toolkit for sequence and polynomial exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone bounded sequence ⇒ convergence; find limit by fixed point
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sequence (an) is monotone (increasing or decreasing) and bounded (above or below), then it has a limit L. That limit L satisfies the fixed-point equation obtained by passing to the limit in the recurrence (replace an, an+1 by L).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction to prove monotonicity and a priori bounds; then set L = f(L) where f is the recurrence function and solve for possible limits. Example: proving an increases and an ≤ 4 ⇒ limit L found by solving L = expression from recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove monotonicity and bounds by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Show an+1 − an has a sign (≥0 or ≤0) and/or compare terms to fixed constants to obtain bounds, then proceed by induction across n to establish monotonicity/boundedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common pattern in many problems: check base cases, assume for n, deduce for n+1. Frequently used to show sequences are increasing/decreasing and to derive bounds like an ≤ C for all n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearize error and use recurrence/characteristic equation to estimate convergence rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Define error sequence xn = |an − L| and derive a linear inequality or linear recurrence relating xn, xn−1, xn−2, etc. Solve the associated characteristic equation; the largest root gives exponential decay rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: derive xn ≤ (1/3)(xn−1 + xn−2) then rewrite as linear recurrence with coefficients and find characteristic roots; the dominant root (λ) determines rate (e.g., slightly larger than 5/8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide-and-average (Newton / Babylonian) iteration: quadratic convergence analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For iteration x_{n+1} = (x_n + a/x_n)/2, possible limits are ±√a; set xn = √a (1 + ε_n) (or other suitable substitution) and analyze ε_{n+1} as a function of ε_n to show quadratic convergence when ε_n small (ε_{n+1} ≈ C ε_n^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For large errors behavior may be linear; for small errors the number of correct digits doubles each iteration. Plug substituted form into iteration and expand to determine order of convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare arithmetic and geometric sequences (AG mean iteration) — monotonicity and difference decay
rubrics_metrics.description: When iterating arithmetic and geometric means an and bn with a0 < b0, then an increases, bn decreases, and an < bn for all n. The difference bn+1 − an+1 is O((bn − an)^2), so the difference decays quadratically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use midpoint and geometric mean inequalities: geometric mean ≤ arithmetic mean and algebraic manipulation to get explicit bounds on bn+1 − an+1 in terms of (bn − an)^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct sequences with prescribed limit-point set via block/bit constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Build sequences by concatenating blocks (e.g., values repeated 2^k times) whose term counts/weights vary so that subsequence ratios converge to any x in a given interval, producing many limit points (e.g., interval [4/3,3/2]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent n in terms of powers of 2 (n = 2^k + m) and derive formulas for an in those blocks; then pass to double limits k,n→∞ and vary m to obtain any limit in an interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model linear recurrences by matrices (shift operator) to deduce divisibility and congruence properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Encode order-2 (or higher) recurrences as linear maps (matrices) T acting on vectors (an−1, an) and use powers of T to study parity/modular properties and divisibility (e.g., factors of 2 in sequence terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute small powers T^k to observe patterns, use induction on matrix entries, and deduce when 2^k divides terms or when entries are ≡1 mod 4, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic equation method for linear homogeneous recurrences
rubrics_metrics.description: For linear recurrences with constant coefficients, form the characteristic polynomial, find its roots λ_i (possibly complex), and express general term as linear combination an = Σ c_i λ_i^n. Use this to get closed-form formulas and asymptotic behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: recurrence an = 3an−1 + 3an−2 − an−3 leads to characteristic λ^3 − 3λ^2 − 3λ + 1; solve for roots and combine with initial conditions. Use parity of roots to deduce squares or multiplicative properties for subsequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use binary (and base-4) expansions to characterize sequence terms / combinatorial structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent integers n in base 2, split odd/even exponents to express numbers as sums of distinct powers of 4 (or other patterns). Use uniqueness of binary representation to deduce uniqueness of such decompositions and classify terms of a sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to identify which integers appear in a sequence or to count representations; e.g., show that except a1=0, terms are sums of distinct powers of 4 via binary splitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescoping transformations for rational-sum simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform kth term expressions into a telescoping form (difference of simpler rational functions), sum over k and collapse to get closed-form partial sums Sn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 1/[k(k+1)(k+2)(k+3)] decomposed into differences yielding Sn = 1/18 − 1/[3(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)].

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove periodicity/nonperiodicity of automatic sequences using substitution rules and binary index relations
rubrics_metrics.description: For sequences generated by morphisms (e.g., Thue–Morse: T:0→01,1→10) or by relations x(2n)=x(n), x(2n+1)=1−x(n), use these self-similarity rules to show invariance under T, deduce relations x(2n)=x(n), and argue ultimate periodicity is impossible or find exact periods if they exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show invariance of infinite word under substitution implies nonperiodicity; use the doubling/bit-flipping recurrences to rule out eventual periodicity of the Thue–Morse sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AM–GM and other classical inequalities to get bounds and monotonicity thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply arithmetic mean–geometric mean inequality and trivial bounds like x + 1/x ≥ 2 to derive lower/upper bounds for sequences, thresholds where sequence becomes monotone, or to show terms remain in an interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using x + 1/x ≥ 2 to deduce a_n^2 growth or employing AM–GM to show x_{n+1} ≤ 5/4 when x_n ≤ 5/4, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modular/period arguments (Euler's theorem) to find periods of integer sequences modulo m
rubrics_metrics.description: When sequence evolution reduces to a linear congruence modulo m (e.g., an+1 ≡ 2 an (mod 1983)), use Euler's theorem and order computations to bound or find exact period (period divides φ(m)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute smallest t with base^t ≡ 1 (mod m) or test divisors; example: period 660 deduced for modulo 661 using φ(661)=660.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove impossibility/contradiction by growth/size arguments (unboundedness contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a contrary boundedness or periodicity property, derive exponential or superlinear growth leading to contradiction with given constraints (e.g., integer size limits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical pattern: show ak ≥ 2^k etc., then a small assumed bound contradicted for some large index (e.g., a100 ≥ 2^100).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational recurrence denominator growth and contradiction for rational sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: For sequences of positive rationals an = pn/qn in lowest terms, analyze how denominators qn evolve (e.g., q_{n+1} ≥ q_n^2) to deduce impossibility of certain behaviors (e.g., existence of infinite rational sequence with given properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If denominators grow too fast integer constraints contradict later rationality/inequalities; show eventual terms cannot remain rational/integer under assumed pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division algorithm for polynomials (existence and uniqueness of quotient and remainder)
rubrics_metrics.description: For polynomials f and g there exist unique q and r such that f(x) = g(x) q(x) + r(x) with deg r < deg g or r = 0. q and r are the quotient and remainder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grade-school polynomial division. Example: x^7 − 1 divided by x^3 + x + 1 yields q(x)=x^4−x^2−x+1 and r(x)=2x^2−2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor theorem: root ⇔ linear factor; multiplicity via repeated factors and derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: f(a)=0 iff (x−a) divides f(x). If f(x) = (x−a)^m q(x) with q(a) ≠ 0 then a is a root of multiplicity m; equivalently f(a)=f'(a)=...=f^{(m−1)}(a)=0 but f^{(m)}(a) ≠ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated factorization or evaluate derivatives at a to determine multiplicity. This criterion is stated explicitly and used for multiplicity detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational Root Test for integer-coefficient polynomials (monic case)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has integer coefficients and z ∈ Z, then f(z)=0 ⇔ z divides the constant term a0. In particular for monic polynomials (leading coefficient 1), any rational root is an integer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If p/q (in lowest terms) is a rational root of integer-coefficient polynomial with leading coefficient 1, then q must equal 1, so p is an integer root dividing a0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vieta's formulas relating roots and coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: For monic polynomials the elementary symmetric sums of roots equal (up to sign) the coefficients: e.g., for x^2 + p x + q, p = −(x1 + x2), q = x1 x2; similar relations for higher degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expansion (x−x1)(x−x2)...(x−xn) to read off coefficients in terms of sums/products of roots; useful in symmetric-sum computations and deriving expressions like x1^2 + x2^2 + x3^2 via (x1 + x2 + x3)^2 − 2 Σ x_i x_j.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra and complete factorization over C
rubrics_metrics.description: Every nonconstant complex-coefficient polynomial has at least one complex root; hence a degree-n polynomial factors into linear factors over C: f(x) = c ∏ (x − x_i) (counting multiplicities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to assert existence of roots and to express polynomials in root form for further algebraic manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roots of unity: factor x^n − 1 and use ω powers for construction and cubic decompositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The nth roots of unity ω^k (ω = e^{2π i/n}) are roots of x^n − 1 and x^n − 1 = ∏_{k=0}^{n−1} (x − ω^k). For cubics, use third roots of unity to factor expressions like x^3 + a^3 + b^3 − 3abx into linear factors involving ω.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use relations 1 + ω + ω^2 = 0 for ω a primitive cube root, and exploit symmetry to express cubic solutions in terms of a and b where a^3, b^3 are roots of a quadratic z^2 − q z − p^3/27.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cubic decomposition (Cardano-flavored) using roots of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: The cubic x^3 − 3ab x + a^3 + b^3 factors as (x + a + b)(x + a ω + b ω^2)(x + a ω^2 + b ω). Comparing with x^3 + p x + q allows to set p = −3ab, q = a^3 + b^3 and reduce solving a cubic to solving a quadratic for a^3 and b^3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute a^3 and b^3 from quadratic z^2 − q z − p^3/27 = 0, then take cube roots to recover a and b and thus the cubic roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trigonometric substitutions and duplication formulas for establishing identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace rational/tangent-like expressions with trigonometric functions and use addition/duplication formulas (e.g., tan 2u = 2 tan u/(1 − tan^2 u)) to transform algebraic identities into angular sum statements, simplifying proofs and enabling induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to triple/trigonometric sequence problems: set x = −tan u etc., infer relations on tan(u+v+w) to propagate algebraic identities to next iteration.
